clue.text: Orwell suggested leaving it up in the air

definitions.text: Orwell suggested leaving it up in the air

parts.words: Orwell suggested leaving it up in the air
parts.note: Orwell's 1936 novel title urges keeping a certain potted houseplant flying, so the plant is what he wanted left aloft

explanation.surface: A remark that Orwell preferred to leave a question unresolved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up in the air' looks like 'undecided', but it is literal: the novel is Keep the Aspidistra Flying.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's novel title names this hardy parlour plant as the thing to be kept flying.

clue.text: Bali destroyed as heretics' home base

indicators.note: destroyed tells us the island's name is broken up and its letters rebuilt

explanation.surface: An Indonesian island laid waste because it sheltered heretics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges BALI. The Albigensian heretics (Cathars) of medieval France took their name from this town.
explanation.definitionFit: The French town gave its name to the Albigensians, a medieval Cathar sect condemned as heretical.

clue.text: Lawrence verses from god that is in ship

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild

indicators.note: in puts the abbreviation for 'that is' inside the letters for a ship

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
i.e. abbreviates id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: D. H. Lawrence's poems taken from a deity on board a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: IE is the abbreviation of Latin id est, 'that is'; SS is a steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: Pansies is the title of a 1929 collection of poems by D. H. Lawrence.

clue.text: Scholar and critic more than once responsible for the Edinburgh Review?

definitions.text: Scholar and critic more than once responsible for the Edinburgh Review?

parts.words: Scholar and critic more than once responsible for the Edinburgh Review?
parts.note: a Scottish literary scholar who wrote and reviewed repeatedly about Edinburgh, with initials doubled like his first name

explanation.surface: A reviewer who kept editing a famous Scottish literary journal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Edinburgh Review is a real journal, but the clue points to a critic who wrote books on Edinburgh; 'more than once' hints at his doubled D initials.
explanation.definitionFit: David Daiches was a Scottish literary scholar and critic who wrote a well-known book on Edinburgh.

clue.text: Hamlet regretted this quality of flesh

definitions.text: Hamlet regretted this quality of flesh

parts.words: Hamlet regretted this quality of flesh
parts.note: Hamlet wishes his 'too too solid flesh would melt', lamenting its firmness

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's prince bemoaning a property of his own body.
explanation.definitionFit: Firmness of substance is the property Hamlet's soliloquy wishes would melt away.

clue.text: Give new title to some books on children American wrote

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is taken, the run lying across two of them

explanation.surface: An American author writing children's books.
explanation.definitionFit: To call something by a different name is to retitle it.

clue.text: A Book by Updike

parts.note: Updike's 1970 work is subtitled 'A Book', after its Jewish novelist protagonist

explanation.surface: Simply a volume written by John Updike.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is the full title, Bech: A Book, minus its first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Bech is Updike's fictional writer, title character of the 1970 story collection.

clue.text: Concluding moves by Beckett

definitions.meaning: the last phase of a chess game

explanation.definitionFit: The final stage of chess play, and the title of Beckett's one-act play.

clue.text: "…he that kills me some six or seven dozen of Scots at a breakfast…" (King Henry IV, Part I) (, )

definitions.text: "…he that kills me some six or seven dozen of Scots at a breakfast…" (King Henry IV, Part I)

parts.words: "…he that kills me some six or seven dozen of Scots at a breakfast…" (King Henry IV, Part I)
parts.note: Prince Hal mocks the bloodthirsty northern rebel nicknamed Hotspur in these words

explanation.surface: A line of Prince Hal's from Shakespeare's history play.
explanation.walkthrough: Hal is describing Hotspur, whose real name is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotspur, the fiery Northumbrian rebel Hal mocks, was Sir Henry Percy.

clue.text: "I believe in —— dictatorships, provided I am the dictator." (Richard Branson)

definitions.text: "I believe in —— dictatorships, provided I am the dictator." (Richard Branson)

parts.words: "I believe in —— dictatorships, provided I am the dictator." (Richard Branson)
parts.note: the missing adjective is the kindly sort of rule Branson jokingly endorses

explanation.surface: A tycoon's joke about autocratic rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindly, well-meaning dictatorships are the sort Branson jokes about leading himself.

clue.text: Overdose fashionable for one-eyed god

parts.note: in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A trendy overdose for a Norse deity.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief Norse deity gave up an eye to drink from the well of wisdom.

clue.text: Spirit of work by

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Spirit of work by (6,6)': the author's name after 'by' is missing, and no source gives the rest.

clue.text: Dryden's 20 church

parts.note: Dryden's allegorical poem casts the Roman church, cross-referenced to 20, as a milk-white female deer

explanation.surface: Dryden's Catholic church, cross-referenced to another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 is CATHOLIC; Dryden's allegorical poem figures the Catholic church as a milk-white female deer, beset by a panther.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dryden's poem a female red deer allegorically stands for the Roman church.

clue.text: E. M. Forster awarded it two cheers

definitions.text: E. M. Forster awarded it two cheers

parts.words: E. M. Forster awarded it two cheers
parts.note: Forster's 1951 essay collection is titled Two Cheers for a system of popular government

explanation.surface: Forster giving a muted cheer to something.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's essay title gives two cheers, not three, to rule by the people.

clue.text: Obscure Victorian hero

parts.note: Hardy's 1895 novel has a stonemason title character called 'the Obscure'

explanation.surface: A forgotten nineteenth-century protagonist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscure' looks like 'little known', but it is the epithet in Hardy's Jude the Obscure.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's stonemason who dreams of Christminster is the protagonist of a Victorian novel.

clue.text: Piers Paul Read featured one such in novel

definitions.text: Piers Paul Read featured one such in novel

parts.words: Piers Paul Read featured one such in novel
parts.note: Read's 1973 novel is titled for a social climber

explanation.surface: A novelist putting a certain type of character in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Read's novel The Upstart centres on a social climber, and the answer is the plural of such parvenus.

clue.text: Essayist as part of chaste electorate

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A writer described as one of a virtuous body of voters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of' picks letters across 'chaSTE ELEctorate'. Richard Steele co-founded The Spectator.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Steele wrote essays for The Tatler and The Spectator.

clue.text: Wildly bids harp to obtain status of wandering minstrel

indicators.note: wildly says the letters of the two words are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A minstrel frantically offering a harp to gain rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -ship makes the position or standing of a bard, a travelling poet-singer.

clue.text: Just one sec provided to sort out violinist

indicators.note: to sort out means the letters of the phrase are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A request for a moment to deal with a fiddler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to sort out' rearranges ONESEC. George Enescu, the Romanian violinist, was often spelt Enesco.
explanation.definitionFit: George Enescu was a Romanian violinist and composer, known in France by the Enesco spelling.

clue.text: "Bid me discourse, I will —— thine ear" (Venus and Adonis)

definitions.text: "Bid me discourse, I will —— thine ear" (Venus and Adonis)

parts.words: "Bid me discourse, I will —— thine ear" (Venus and Adonis)
parts.note: Venus promises to bewitch Adonis's hearing with her talk

explanation.surface: Venus offering to charm Adonis with words.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus vows to delight and bewitch Adonis's hearing.

clue.text: Universal nature of one of Brian Moore's eponymous characters

definitions.text: one of Brian Moore's eponymous characters
definitions.meaning: Moore's 1972 novella is titled for members of the Roman church

explanation.definitionFit: The word means all-embracing, and Moore's novella Catholics is named for followers of Rome.

clue.text: Attractive German singer from Koblenz

parts.note: the legendary siren of a Rhine rock upstream of Koblenz lured boatmen to their doom

explanation.surface: An alluring vocalist from a Rhineland city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine siren of legend sang from her rock near Koblenz, luring sailors to wreck.

clue.text: Devout emperor playwright

parts.note: pi is slang for pious, devout
Nero was a Roman emperor

explanation.surface: A pious emperor who wrote plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Wing Pinero was a Victorian dramatist.

clue.text: Carelessly displace a Greek verse form

indicators.note: carelessly says the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone misplacing a Greek line of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A classical metre named after the Greek poet Asclepiades.

clue.text: A mate of 12's, perhaps, as well as Kaufman

definitions.meaning: 12 is a female deer, whose partner is a male red deer
Moss of that name co-wrote plays with George S. Kaufman

explanation.definitionFit: A stag partners a female deer, and Moss Hart was Kaufman's playwriting collaborator.

clue.text: How did Zarathustra speak?

indicators.note: speak, with the question, hints the reply is found within the prophet's own name

explanation.surface: A question about Nietzsche's prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: The reply sits inside 'Zarathustra' itself, and Nietzsche's title gives it: in this way spake Zarathustra.
explanation.definitionFit: Nietzsche's book title gives the manner of the prophet's speaking, 'in this way'.

clue.text: Vigorous move made at last by Thomas Hobbes

definitions.text: Vigorous move made at last by Thomas Hobbes

parts.words: Vigorous move made at last by Thomas Hobbes
parts.note: Hobbes's reported dying words spoke of a great jump in the dark

explanation.surface: The philosopher finally doing something energetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last' means at his death: Hobbes reputedly said he was about to take 'a great leap in the dark'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hobbes's last words called death a great jump into the dark.

clue.text: Enduring character from Genesis

parts.note: the Genesis patriarch lived 969 years, longest of anyone in the Bible

explanation.surface: A long-lasting figure from the first book of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical patriarch lived 969 years, so his name stands for great longevity.

clue.text: Fictional character inspiring much research in high places

definitions.text: Fictional character inspiring much research in high places

parts.words: Fictional character inspiring much research in high places
parts.note: the Himalayan snowman, possibly fictional, has prompted many mountain expeditions

explanation.surface: A made-up figure prompting study among the powerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High places' looks like government, but it is the Himalayas, where expeditions hunt the abominable snowman.
explanation.definitionFit: The abominable snowman may be a myth, yet expeditions keep searching Himalayan heights for it.

clue.text: Neoplatonist capable of the purple passage?

definitions.text: Neoplatonist capable of the purple passage?

parts.words: Neoplatonist capable of the purple passage?
parts.note: the philosopher's Greek name means 'clad in purple', so he might write florid prose

explanation.surface: A philosopher able to write ornate prose.
explanation.walkthrough: Porphyry the Neoplatonist was named from Greek porphyra, purple; a purple passage is florid writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Porphyry, Latin Porphyrius, was a third-century Neoplatonist whose name means purple.
